newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's hard-left rattles sabre on welfare reforms.
newsitem.headline: Italy's hard-left rattles sabre on welfare reforms.

text.p: Talks to reform Italy's welfare system will not get off the ground unless the government rules out spending cuts, hard-left Communist Refoundation leader Fausto Bertinotti said at the weekend.

Bertinotti, whose party's support is crucial to Prime Minister Romano Prodi's centre-left coalition in the lower house of parliament, was asked by the daily newspaper La Repubblica whether he would sit down at the negotiating table to work out welfare reforms.
"If the idea of making cuts is ruled out beforehand..." he told the newspaper's Sunday edition.

The government, which last week unveiled a 15.5 trillion lire mini-budget ($9.2 billion), is under fire from industry and opposition alike for tinkering with accounting methods and not tackling long-term welfare and pension system spending.
They and economists argue Italy must make structural reforms to state expenditure to meet and maintain tough economic criteria for European economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999.

Prodi said last week an eventual reform will be enshrined in the 1998 budget but admitted he faced an uphill battle, saying: "I do not have the backing of anyone...it will be a hard and tough discussion."
Bertinotti last week backed the additional deficit-cutting measures because they met his demands for no new taxes and no reduction in welfare spending.

But he said at the weekend he wanted the ruling coalition to dismiss the idea right from the start that future welfare reforms would contain spending cuts, because Italy's social spending was lower than the European average and tax evasion higher.
Defence of the welfare state "must be stated at the start."

"This is not an uninfluential but a determining factor to establish the terms of the debate. If you're in Rome and you start on a trip, you have to know whether the journey is going to take you to Milan or Naples," he said.
"We have to see whether all those who want to go to Milan and those who want to go to Naples actually move at the starter's gun, or whether there's a selection beforehand."
But Foreign Trade Minister Augusto Fantozzi told La Repubblica reform talks would go ahead with or without Bertinotti once local council elections on April 27 were over.

"To sit at the reform table only if the idea of cuts is ruled out beforehand is an ultimatum which reveals how little will there is to sit down at the table," said Fantozzi, a former finance minister and part of the centrist Italian Renewal party in the ruling coalition.

Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi, rejecting criticism that last week's mini-budget was harmful to Italy's economy and credibility, said on Monday the measure was the "quantitative" part of a two-step economic policy and added the government was determined to address welfare reforms.

"Last Thursday the prime minister solemnly and publicly undertook to deal with the qualitative aspects as well, to open up the necessary debate as soon as possible with the parties concerned," Ciampi wrote in a reply to public criticism from Nobel Prize winning economist Franco Modigliani.
The mini-budget has been fiercely attacked by the business federation Confindustria who want it withdrawn, arguing that it could cripple industry and raise unemployment. $1=1,674 lire
